Item four concerned the recycling scheme introduced in the spring, and a briefing note circulated to members set out the tonnages collected in each of the first six months. Officers explained that the weight of dry recyclables had risen steadily while residual waste had fallen, a pattern they attributed partly to the smaller bins issued to every household and partly to the fortnightly collection of food waste. Several members asked about contamination rates, and the officer confirmed that the share of rejected material had dropped from eleven per cent to just under six. A resident speaking from the public gallery described the smell from the communal bins behind the flats on Mill Road during the hot spell in July, and asked whether the collection schedule could be adjusted in summer. The chair invited the waste manager to respond, and he promised to revisit the route timings before the next meeting. The finance officer then presented the cost figures: the scheme had come in slightly under budget, mainly because the vehicle fleet had needed fewer repairs than forecast. A question followed about staffing, and members were told that two additional loaders had been recruited on temporary contracts. The discussion moved to publicity, and the communications lead reported that leaflets had gone to every address and that a short video had been watched about four thousand times. One member asked whether the leaflet had been translated, and was told that it had been printed in six languages and that the library kept copies in the foyer. A member asked whether compostable liners would be supplied free of charge from April, and the officer said the details were still being negotiated with the contractor, who had asked for another round of talks before signing. The chair noted that the contract would return to the committee in September and asked members to send further questions to the clerk in writing. Outside, the rain had stopped, and a few people lingered in the corridor reading the papers. The chair then turned to the final item, the annual residents' survey, carried out in June by an independent research company. The company had posted questionnaires to a random sample of households and followed up by telephone where no reply arrived. The response rate was described as respectable for a survey of this kind, and the sample was weighted to match the age profile of the borough. Members were shown a slide summarising the headline measures. On the whole, residents were reasonably satisfied with the reliability of the collections and with the condition in which the bins were left, though satisfaction was markedly lower among households in flats than among those in houses. The slide also reported how easy people found the collection calendar and whether they had ever needed to report a missed collection. A member asked how the results compared with the previous year, and the officer said that most measures had held steady, with a small improvement in the rating for customer service and a modest rise in the performance score for the garden waste service. The chair thanked the officers and asked that the full tables be circulated before the next meeting. The meeting closed at twenty past nine, and the members drifted out into a cool, damp evening, some of them still arguing about the bins.
